questions.title: Modules & Imports practice 1
questions.prompt: Which line makes the `random` module available under its own name?
choices: import random
from random import randint
include random
using random
questions.explanation: `import random` binds the module name. Its functions are then reached with a dot, such as `random.randint(1, 6)`.

questions.title: Modules & Imports practice 2
choices: When this file is run directly
Every time the file is imported
Only after an error
Before Python reads the file
questions.explanation: Python sets `__name__` to `"__main__"` for the file that starts the program. Imported modules receive their module names instead.

questions.title: Trace Modules & Imports
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: Importing the module keeps the source of `sqrt` clear. The dot says that the function comes from math. The resulting output is '5.0'.

questions.title: Modules & Imports practice 5
questions.prompt: Why prefer `import math; math.sqrt(16)` over `from math import *`?
choices: The wildcard dumps every name in and can quietly overwrite one you defined
The wildcard import is a syntax error
math.sqrt is faster than sqrt
sqrt does not exist in the math module
questions.explanation: `from math import *` pulls in every public name at once, which hides where a name came from and can shadow something you already defined (for example, your own `sqrt`). `import math` keeps the boundary visible: `math.sqrt` says exactly where it lives. Both call the same function at the same speed.

questions.title: Import side effects
questions.prompt: What happens to top-level statements in a Python file when another file imports it?
choices: They run during the import.
They run only when a function from the file is called.
They are ignored unless the file has no functions.
They are converted into comments.
questions.explanation: Importing a module executes its top-level code once so Python can create the module's names. That is why direct prompts, print demos, or long-running work should not sit loose at the top level when the file is meant to be imported.

questions.title: Module purpose
questions.prompt: A file named `grade_utils.py` is growing. What should guide what belongs in it?
choices: Put every helper from the project into the same file.
Group functions that share one clear purpose.
Move code there only because it is currently broken.
Use the file as a place for random experiments and user input.
questions.explanation: A module is easiest to use when its contents share a purpose. `grade_utils.py` should hold grade-related helpers, not every unrelated tool. Clear grouping makes imports easier to read and keeps files from becoming cluttered.

questions.title: Readable imports
questions.prompt: Why can `import math` followed by `math.sqrt(16)` be clearer than `from math import *`?
choices: Wildcard imports make Python run faster.
Wildcard imports prevent name conflicts automatically.
The module name shows where `sqrt` came from.
The module name makes `sqrt` return a string.
questions.explanation: Using the module name keeps the source of the function visible at the call site. Wildcard imports can hide where names came from and can accidentally overwrite names from other imports. Readable imports help future debugging.

questions.title: Avoid wildcard imports
questions.prompt: What is a common problem with `from module import *`?
choices: It imports nothing unless the module has a class.
It forces every function call to use a module prefix.
It prevents the file from being tested.
It fills the namespace with names whose source is hard to see.
questions.explanation: Wildcard imports pull many names into the current file without showing them individually. That can make it hard to tell which module supplied a name and can create accidental conflicts. Explicit imports are usually easier for beginners and reviewers to follow.

questions.title: Top-level work
questions.prompt: What kind of work is safest to leave at the top level of an importable module?
choices: Small definitions such as constants, functions, and classes.
A required input prompt that starts as soon as the module imports.
A long file download that runs on every import.
A demo loop that prints examples before any function is called.
questions.explanation: Top-level definitions are normal because importing the module needs to create those names. Interactive prompts, demos, and expensive work are surprising during import. Put that behavior in a function or behind a main guard.

questions.title: Main guard
choices: It makes imports impossible from other files.
It lets the demo run when the file is executed directly, but not when the file is imported.
It makes every function private.
It changes the file extension from `.py` to a package.
questions.explanation: The main guard separates reusable module code from direct-run demo code. When the file is imported, `__name__` is the module name, so the guarded demo does not run. When the file is run directly, the demo can still execute.
